slides.title: The rwnd Formula
slides.body:
Free Buffer = rwnd
rwnd (Receive Window)
TCP sends multiple segments without waiting for individual ACKs — but the sender needs a limit. That limit comes from the receiver’s available buffer space. The receiver measures this free space and sends it to the sender. This value is called rwnd (Receive Window)
The sending rule is:  Bytes in flight  ≤  rwnd

slides.title: The rwnd Formula
slides.body:
Free Buffer = rwnd
The Formula: 
rwnd = Receive Buffer Size − (LastByteReceived − LastByteRead)
LastByteReceived      last byte that arrived from the network into the buffer
LastByteRead     last byte the application consumed via recv()
LastByteReceived − LastByteRead = occupied buffer space
Buffer Size minus occupied space = free space = rwnd

slides.title: Duplicate ACKs
slides.body:
Receiver sends ACK for the next expected byte
If a segment is missing, ACK cannot advance
Out-of-order segments arrive → receiver keeps ACKing the same byte
These repeated ACKs are Duplicate ACKs
Detecting Packet Loss

slides.title: Duplicate ACKs
slides.body:
Detecting Packet Loss
Suppose the sender transmits Seg-1, Seg-2, Seg-3, Seg-4, Seg-5. Seg-2 is lost
Seg-3 arrives → gap at Seg-2 → Dup ACK (Ack = 1001) — “still waiting for byte 1001”
Seg-4 arrives → gap still present → Dup ACK (Ack = 1001)
Seg-5 arrives → gap still present → Dup ACK (Ack = 1001)
The sender receives 3 consecutive duplicate ACKs for byte 1001

slides.title: Duplicate ACKs
slides.body:

3 Dup ACKs
What it likely means?
Could be normal packet reordering — very common
Still ambiguous — reordering is still possible
Statistically reliable signal of genuine loss (RFC 5681)

No action

slides.title: Duplicate ACKs
slides.body:
Detecting Packet Loss
Critical observation:
Seg-3, Seg-4, Seg-5 are arriving at the receiver. Only Seg-2 is missing. The network path is working — this is an isolated, mild loss event. The response should be proportional
Contrast with Timeout:
The response to each is very different — Fast Retransmit handles the mild case, Timeout triggers a full reset

slides.title: Congestion Control
slides.body:
Sender Protects the Network
Network also has limits → excess traffic fills router buffers → packet loss
Congestion Control handles this (different from flow control)
TCP infers congestion from loss/delay — no explicit signal
Uses cwnd (Congestion Window) to regulate sending
Rule: Bytes in flight ≤ cwnd

slides.title: Congestion Control
slides.body:
Sender Protects the Network
Dropped packets trigger retransmissions

slides.title: Congestion Control
slides.body: Sender Protects the Network

slides.title: Congestion Window
slides.body:
Sender’s Network Estimate
cwnd - Congestion Window
Maintained only at sender (not shared with receiver)
Limits how much data can be safely in flight
Starts small → grows as network handles more
Shrinks on congestion detection
TCP needs its own estimate of network capacity, independent of the receiver. This is cwnd — Congestion Window

slides.title: Congestion Window
slides.body:
Sender’s Network Estimate
rwnd = “how much the receiver can accept” (receiver-controlled)
cwnd = “how much the network can carry” (sender-estimated)
The sender uses whichever is smaller
Both rwnd and cwnd constrain the sender simultaneously:  Bytes in flight  ≤  min(rwnd, cwnd)

slides.title: Slow Start
slides.body:
Building cwnd From Zero
At start, TCP doesn’t know network capacity → full send risks congestion
Slow Start begins with cwnd = 1 MSS
Grows exponentially: each RTT, ACKs increase cwnd → doubles per RTT
Quickly reaches usable capacity without staying too slow

slides.body:

slides.title: Fast Retransmit
slides.body:
No Timer — Retransmit Now
Seg-3, 4, 5 arrived — network is live, only Seg-2 missing → response must be proportional, not severe
Without Fast Recovery: TCP resets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts Slow Start — severe overreaction to an isolated drop
With Fast Recovery: cwnd halves, TCP skips Slow Start & resumes Congestion Avoidance directly

TCP error control operates entirely at the endpoints. Two mechanisms cover segment loss:

slides.title: Jacobson’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Adaptive RTO from RTT
Mechanism
RTT
SRTT
Trigger
Time from sending to receiving ACK — changes constantly
Smoothed average — absorbs spikes
Response
—
(1−0.125)×SRTT + 0.125×RTTsample
RTTVAR
RTT fluctuation — high = unpredictable network
(1 − 0.25) × RTTVAR + 0.25 × |SRTT − RTTsample|
RTO = SRTT + 4 × RTTVAR [Min = 1 second]
RTO = the timer TCP starts when it sends a segment. If no ACK before expiry → retransmit. Must adapt to network conditions

slides.title: Karn’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Retransmission Ambiguity Fix
The Problem:
When a segment is retransmitted and an ACK arrives, TCP cannot tell: 
Was the ACK for the original segment? → RTT = time since original send
Was the ACK for the retransmitted copy? → RTT = time since retransmission
Using the wrong value corrupts SRTT — making RTO too short or too long

slides.title: Karn’s Algorithm
slides.body:
Retransmission Ambiguity Fix
Karn’s Solution (RFC 6298):
Rule 1
Do not measure RTT from retransmitted segments. Only use segments sent exactly once
Rule 2
Exponential Backoff: After each timeout, double the RTO:
RTO = 2 × RTO  (on each consecutive timeout)
